summary: Considers what a host should do when a message sent over the early network does not get a normal reply. The IMP can return different message types depending on whether the destination IMP or its host interface is down. It suggests how to handle those cases and time-outs.

eli5.summary: When you send a letter and nothing comes back, you wonder if the address is wrong or the person is away. This note lists the signals and what to do for each.

questions: how should a host handle time-outs in the host-host protocol
what happens when a destination imp is down
how do you recover from lost connections
why do network connections get stuck
subtitle: Detecting and recovering from lost connections in early network protocols

tldr.problem: When a host sends a command over the network and gets no reply, resources (sockets, buffers) remain tied up because the host-host protocol has no time-out mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes adding a time-out to the Host-Host Protocol: if no matching response arrives within a fixed time T, the sending host assumes the response is lost, closes the connection, and frees the resources.
tldr.outcome: A time-out allows hosts to detect dead or slow remote hosts and reclaim resources instead of waiting forever.

facts.label: Problem
facts.value: Resources tied up indefinitely when no response arrives

today: RFC 142 proposed adding timeouts to the Host-Host Protocol. This became a foundational principle for TCP and other transport protocols, which implement retransmission timeouts to recover from lost packets and unresponsive hosts.

sections.title: The Problem: Resources Stuck in Limbo
sections.content: When the NCP (Network Control Program) on one host sends a connection request (STR or RTS) or a close command (CLS) to a remote host and receives no response, the sending host stays in a waiting state. The sockets, table space, and buffers for that connection cannot be reused because the connection is still technically open. If the remote host is down, hung, or simply not responding, these resources will be tied up indefinitely.
sections.eli5: If you send a command and wait forever for an answer that never comes, you cannot move on to the next thing.

sections.title: The Solution: Time-Out Mechanism
sections.content: The solution is a timer T, a network-wide standard timeout value. On sending an STR or RTS, if no matching response arrives in T time units, the host sends a close command and assumes the connection is dead. On sending a close command, if no matching close arrives in T time units, the host assumes it is received and frees the resources. This prevents the host from being stuck indefinitely.
sections.eli5: Wait a fixed amount of time for an answer. If it does not come, assume it is lost, clean up, and move on.

sections.title: A Timing Question Remains
sections.content: The RFC identifies a subtle race condition: if a close command times out and is assumed to have arrived, but a new STR arrives on the same socket pair shortly after, and then the original close finally arrives, there is no way to tell which command the incoming close is answering. The author brings this to the attention of the Host-Host Protocol committee. The value of T itself must be decided as a network standard; no specific time is recommended in this early RFC.
sections.eli5: One tricky question remains: if two close commands get mixed up, how do we know which one matched? The note flags this for the protocol team to solve.
